c.tagline: Iraq's holiest pilgrimage city, where two golden shrines face each other.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are rarely used; agree the fare with the driver before setting off, or share a per-seat 'service' taxi on fixed routes. App-based ride-hailing coverage is thin, and during Arba'een most pilgrims cross the shrine district on foot.

emergency.note: National emergency line 112; fire 115. Ambulance service can be limited, so private hospitals or your embassy's line may be faster. Security is heavy around the shrines.

avoid.reason: Stay within the well-secured shrine city and main routes; avoid rural desert areas toward the Anbar border due to residual security risks.
Around the Imam Hussein and Abbas shrines, dense pilgrimage crowds bring pickpocketing and crush risk, and expect frequent security checkpoints requiring your passport.

hood_desc: The dense historic core wrapped around the Imam Husayn Shrine, with the covered bazaar, religious schools and the highest concentration of guesthouses; convenient but very crowded during Muharram and Arba'een.
A newer, more spread-out residential quarter east of the shrines with modern hotels and lower rates; quieter and a short taxi ride from the holy sites.
The area around the historic Baghdad Gate on the northern edge of the old town, full of markets, cheap eateries and transport links, within walking distance of the shrines.
A calmer suburban district southwest toward Najaf, built around the domed shrine of Hurr ibn Yazid al-Riyahi; residential and green, popular for a quieter stay away from the crowds.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash directly to the driver; there is no rechargeable transit card. Shared 'service' taxis on fixed routes are far more common than public buses and are paid per seat in dinars.
transit.hours: Buses and shared taxis run roughly 6am-10pm; after that, private taxis fill the gap.
transit.note: Public transit is minimal; most pilgrims and residents rely on shared service taxis, private cars and walking. Foot traffic around the shrines is enormous, and during Arba'een the whole shrine district becomes a pedestrian zone.

train: Iraqi Republic Railways runs limited pilgrimage-season services linking Baghdad and Karbala
bus: Intercity buses and shared 'service' taxis to Najaf (~80 km), Baghdad (~100 km) and Hillah from the city's garages

transit.m: Shared 'service' taxi or pilgrim coach to Karbala (~1.5 hr)

tip.r: Not expected; rounding up a taxi or restaurant bill is appreciated. Much service around the shrines is driven by hospitality to pilgrims rather than tipping.

food.name: Timman qeema

landmarks: Imam Husayn Shrine
The golden-domed mausoleum of the Prophet's grandson, martyred at Karbala in 680 AD, draws millions of Shia pilgrims in the world's largest gatherings.
Al-Abbas Shrine
The resplendent gold-and-turquoise shrine of Abbas ibn Ali, Husayn's valiant standard-bearer, whose mirrored halls shimmer with devotion and Quranic calligraphy.
Bayn al-Haramayn (Between the Two Shrines)
The vast marble esplanade linking the two holy shrines becomes an ocean of humanity during Ashura and the epic Arbaeen pilgrimage.
Al-Ukhaidir Fortress
A monumental 8th-century Abbasid desert palace southwest of Karbala, its towering walls and vaulted halls astonishingly intact amid empty sands.
Khaymagah (Camp of Imam Husayn)
A revered memorial marking where Husayn's family pitched their tents before the Battle of Karbala, its chambers evoking the tragedy's opening hours.
Tell al-Zaynabiya (Zaynab's Hill)
The small mound from which Lady Zaynab is said to have watched the battle unfold, now a poignant station on every pilgrim's route.
Shrine of Al-Hurr al-Riyahi
The tomb of the enemy commander who famously changed sides to die beside Husayn, standing amid orchards west of the city.
Karbala Old City Souks
Bustling covered bazaars around the shrines perfume the air with rosewater, dates and prayer beads, serving pilgrims from every continent.
Lake Razzaza (Milh Lake)
Iraq's second-largest lake spreads glassy and shallow west of Karbala, a desert-edge escape for birdwatching, fishing and sunset picnics.
Maqam of Imam al-Mahdi
A graceful riverside sanctuary on the Husseiniya channel dedicated to the awaited twelfth Imam, popular for quiet evening devotions.

dom.op: Iraqi Republic Railways (IRR) — tickets sold at station ticket offices only; there is no online booking

train.note: A new line to Karbala was built in recent years and one or two trains a week run from Baghdad and from Basra, with extra services laid on for Ashura and Arbaeen when millions of pilgrims converge on the city. Departures are irregular and tickets can only be bought at station counters from Iraqi Republic Railways, so the train is a curiosity rather than a dependable way in - buses and shared taxis run all day. Iraq has had no scheduled international passenger trains since 2003, and the Basra-Shalamcheh link towards Iran remains unfinished.

intl.to: Mehran & Tehran, Qom, Mashhad (Iran) - pilgrimage coaches via the Mehran/Zurbatiyah and Shalamcheh/Basra crossings
intl.op: Iranian and Iraqi pilgrimage coach operators — booked through pilgrimage agencies rather than online

bus.note: Karbala has no functioning airport, so almost everyone arrives by road: coaches and shared taxis from Baghdad take about 2 hours, Najaf about 1.5 hours and Basra most of a day, and they use the garages on the approach roads because vehicles cannot enter the shrine precinct. Buying is done at the counter or direct with the driver; there is no meaningful online booking on the Iraqi side. The heaviest international traffic is Iranian pilgrim coaches crossing at Mehran, and during Arbaeen the road system is effectively rebuilt around the pilgrimage, with free transport, road closures and journey times several times longer than normal. Visitors should check current visa rules, as Iraqi visa-on-arrival policy has changed repeatedly.

ferry.note: Karbala sits on the edge of the desert well inland from the Euphrates channel and has no port or navigable waterway, so there are no ferry services.

half.name: Najaf
half.blurb: The Imam Ali Shrine and the vast Wadi al-Salam cemetery, one of the largest in the world, sit in this Shia holy city.

half.name: Hillah / Babylon
half.blurb: Reconstructed sections of the ancient city of Babylon, including the Ishtar Gate replica and ruins of Nebuchadnezzar's palace, lie near this city.
